### ⚠️ Exact P-Values {#exact-p-values .red} We found 5 imprecise *p* values out of 44 detected *p* values.
View detailed feedback Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold"). ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::
::: {.callout-note title="How It Works" collapse="true"} List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000). This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001. A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note ("* p < .05, ** p < .01"), a figure legend ("Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)", "Values in bold are significant at p < .05") or a stated threshold ("p < .05 was considered significant", "thresholded at p < .001"). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a ";" or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it ("F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05"). The column `not_a_test` of the table says why a p-value was left out ("marker", "threshold", "legend" or "named"). A p-value with the name of a correction or a test after the p ("pFWE < .05", "padj < 0.05", "p Wilcoxon = .02") is flagged only when a test statistic comes before it in its clause ("t(37) = 7.17, p FWE < .05"). Without one it is mostly the rule that decided what was significant ("genes with padj < 0.05 were selected"); such a p-value is "named" in `not_a_test`. Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value ("p < .05 (*)"), are still flagged. This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold ("decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold"). This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table's footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above). This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens Read more in the [metacheck manual](https://www.scienceverse.org/metacheck_book/chapters/mod-stat-p-exact.html). ::: ::: {.validation} Validation: Validated on 226 Psychological Science papers with 5,019 hand-coded p-values, 438 of them imprecise (scienceverse/validation, branch stat_p_exact). Version 0.4.4.3 reported 419 p-values as imprecise, 388 of them correctly (93%), and missed 50 (89% found). Of the misses, 13 are starred table notes ("*p < .05") that the module leaves out on purpose and 11 are p-values it did not find; of the wrong reports, 20 are p-values the ground truth does not contain (such as "ps < .05") and 6 use ≤ or ≥. These figures measure agreement with the hand-coding, which has known errors in both directions (scienceverse/validation#48). :::
